questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Leaving out palladium, which is an exception, the general outer electronic configuration of the d-block elements is:

solution.concept: Electronic configuration of the d-block elements
solution.explanation: In the d-block, the (n−1)d orbitals are being filled while the outermost ns orbital holds one or two electrons. Palladium (4d¹⁰ 5s⁰) is the exception NCERT mentions.
steps: d-block: inner (n−1)d subshell filled progressively, d¹ to d¹⁰
Outer ns subshell: 1 or 2 electrons (e.g. Cr 3d⁵ 4s¹, Fe 3d⁶ 4s²)
solution.why_others_wrong: ns² np¹⁻⁶ is the p-block configuration. (n−2)f¹⁻¹⁴ (n−1)d⁰⁻¹ ns² is the f-block (inner transition) configuration. (n−1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns⁰ fits only palladium, the stated exception.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', electronic configurations of the d-block elements

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The spin-only magnetic moment of the V³⁺ ion (Z of V = 23) is about:

solution.explanation: V is [Ar] 3d³ 4s². Removing the two 4s electrons and one 3d electron leaves V³⁺ = [Ar] 3d², with two unpaired electrons.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.73 BM is for one unpaired electron. 3.87 BM is for three (V²⁺, 3d³). 4.90 BM is for four unpaired electrons.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', magnetic properties (spin-only formula)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Samarium (Z = 62) has the configuration [Xe] 4f⁶ 6s². The number of 4f electrons in the Sm³⁺ ion is:

solution.explanation: To form Ln³⁺, the two 6s electrons are lost first and then one 4f electron (there is no 5d electron in Sm).
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 is the 4f count of the neutral atom (or of Sm²⁺). 3 confuses the charge with the 4f count. 8 is Z − 54 without removing any electrons.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', the lanthanoids (electronic configurations)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The electronic configuration of lanthanum (Z = 57) is [Xe] 4f¹ 6s².
Statement II: Yb²⁺, which has a 4f¹⁴ configuration, acts as a reducing agent.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Configurations and oxidation states of the lanthanoids
solution.explanation: Lanthanum is [Xe] 5d¹ 6s²; its 4f subshell is empty. NCERT notes that Yb²⁺ (f¹⁴), like Eu²⁺, is a reductant, changing to the common +3 state.
steps: Statement II: Yb²⁺ (4f¹⁴) is oxidised to Yb³⁺, so it is a reducing agent → true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', the lanthanoids (electronic configurations, oxidation states)
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 25.0 mL of 0.10 M sodium sulphite solution is oxidised to sulphate by acidified 0.020 M KMnO₄ solution (permanganate is reduced to Mn²⁺). The volume of KMnO₄ solution needed is:

solution.explanation: MnO₄⁻ gains 5 electrons (Mn +7 → +2) and SO₃²⁻ loses 2 electrons (S +4 → +6), so 2 MnO₄⁻ react with 5 SO₃²⁻: 2MnO₄⁻ + 5SO₃²⁻ + 6H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 5SO₄²⁻ + 3H₂O.
solution.shortcut: Equivalents: 2.5 × 2 = 5 meq of sulphite = 0.020 × 5 × V → V = 50 mL.
solution.why_others_wrong: 125 mL takes a 1 : 1 mole ratio. 83.3 mL treats permanganate as gaining 3 electrons (reduction to MnO₂, which happens only in neutral solution). 312.5 mL inverts the 2 : 5 ratio.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', potassium permanganate (oxidising action in acid solution)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The second ionisation enthalpies of chromium and copper are unusually high compared with those of their neighbours in the 3d series.
Reason (R): Removing the second electron from Cr⁺ (3d⁵) or Cu⁺ (3d¹⁰) breaks up a stable half-filled or completely filled d subshell.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Irregularities in the ionisation enthalpies of the 3d series
solution.explanation: After the first ionisation, Cr⁺ is 3d⁵ and Cu⁺ is 3d¹⁰. NCERT points out that the second ionisation enthalpies are higher for Cr and Cu precisely because these M⁺ ions have the stable d⁵ and d¹⁰ configurations, which must be disturbed.
steps: The second electron must come from the stable d⁵ / d¹⁰ set → high IE₂ (A true)
R states exactly this cause → R explains A
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', ionisation enthalpies
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match the species in List-I with its ground-state electronic configuration in List-II (atomic numbers: Cr 24, Fe 26, Co 27, Zn 30).

List-I:
A. Cr
B. Zn²⁺
C. Fe³⁺
D. Co³⁺

List-II:
I. [Ar] 3d⁶
II. [Ar] 3d⁵
III. [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹
IV. [Ar] 3d¹⁰

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Chromium takes the half-filled 3d⁵ 4s¹ arrangement. Ions of the 3d metals lose their 4s electrons first.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-II, C-III gives Fe³⁺ a 4s electron, but 4s electrons are lost first. C-I, D-II swaps the d counts of Fe³⁺ and Co³⁺. B-II, C-IV mixes up Zn²⁺ and Fe³⁺.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', electronic configurations
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the metals of the 3d series are correct?

(a) The atomic radii decrease at first along the series and then change very little for the middle elements.
(b) The density of the metals generally increases from titanium to copper.
(c) Zinc has the highest enthalpy of atomisation in the series.
(d) Metals with very high enthalpies of atomisation tend to be noble in their reactions.
(e) Ti⁴⁺ compounds are coloured because Ti⁴⁺ has unpaired 3d electrons.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Radii fall at first and then level off in the middle (Fe, Co, Ni are almost the same size), so density rises from Ti to Cu as mass increases. Zinc, with no unpaired d electrons, has the lowest enthalpy of atomisation. Ti⁴⁺ is 3d⁰, so its compounds are colourless (white TiO₂).
steps: (a) radii decrease, then nearly constant → true
(c) Zn has the lowest, not highest, enthalpy of atomisation → false
(d) high atomisation enthalpy → noble behaviour (NCERT) → true
(e) Ti⁴⁺ is d⁰, no unpaired electrons → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Each other option includes (c) or (e), which are false, or leaves out a true statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', physical properties, atomic sizes, enthalpies of atomisation

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The actinoids show a greater range of oxidation states than the lanthanoids. This is attributed mainly to the fact that:

options.text: the 5f orbitals are buried more deeply in the atom than the 4f orbitals
the 5f, 6d and 7s levels are of comparable energies
the actinoid contraction is smaller than the lanthanoid contraction

solution.explanation: Because the 5f, 6d and 7s levels lie close in energy, a variable number of electrons can be used in bonding, so the actinoids show many oxidation states.
steps: Range of oxidation states depends on how many electrons can be removed at similar cost
5f, 6d and 7s are of comparable energies → variable oxidation states
solution.why_others_wrong: The 5f orbitals are less deeply buried than 4f, not more, so the first option is reversed. Radioactivity does not decide oxidation states. The actinoid contraction is in fact greater from element to element, and in any case contraction does not explain the range.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', the actinoids (oxidation states)
solution.final_answer: Option B: the 5f, 6d and 7s levels are of comparable energies

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In neutral solution, in the presence of zinc sulphate, permanganate oxidises Mn²⁺ ions to MnO₂ and is itself reduced to MnO₂. When 0.020 mol of MnO₄⁻ reacts completely with Mn²⁺ in this way, the total mass of MnO₂ formed is (Mn = 55, O = 16):

solution.explanation: MnO₄⁻ (+7) gains 3 electrons and Mn²⁺ loses 2 electrons, both ending at +4. Balancing electrons: 2MnO₄⁻ + 3Mn²⁺ + 2H₂O → 5MnO₂ + 4H⁺. Both reactants end up as MnO₂.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.74 g counts only the MnO₂ coming from permanganate, and 2.61 g only that from Mn²⁺. 3.48 g assumes a 1 : 1 ratio of MnO₄⁻ to Mn²⁺.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', potassium permanganate (oxidising action in neutral solution)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about potassium permanganate and potassium dichromate are correct?

(a) In neutral or faintly alkaline solution, each MnO₄⁻ ion gains three electrons.
(b) In acidic solution, each Cr₂O₇²⁻ ion gains six electrons.
(c) The manganate and permanganate ions are both tetrahedral.
(d) Commercially, manganate is converted into permanganate by electrolytic oxidation in alkaline solution.
(e) In acidic solution, one MnO₄⁻ ion oxidises three Fe²⁺ ions.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Structures and electron changes of permanganate and dichromate
solution.explanation: MnO₄⁻ → MnO₂ in neutral/faintly alkaline solution is +7 → +4 (3e⁻). Cr₂O₇²⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ is 2 × 3 = 6e⁻. Both MnO₄²⁻ and MnO₄⁻ are tetrahedral. Industrially, MnO₂ is fused with alkali and an oxidant to give manganate, which is then oxidised electrolytically to permanganate in alkaline solution. In acid, MnO₄⁻ gains 5e⁻ and so oxidises five Fe²⁺ ions.
solution.why_others_wrong: Any option containing (e) is wrong; (a), (c), (d) only leaves out the true statement (b).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', potassium dichromate and potassium permanganate

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): MnO is a basic oxide, whereas Mn₂O₇ is an acidic oxide.
Reason (R): As the oxidation state of a metal increases, the ionic character of its oxides decreases and their acidic character increases.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Nature of the oxides of transition metals
solution.explanation: In MnO, manganese is +2 and the oxide is ionic and basic. In Mn₂O₇ (+7, a covalent green oil) the oxide is acidic, giving permanganic acid. NCERT relates this to the fall in ionic character with rising oxidation state.
steps: Higher oxidation state → less ionic, more acidic oxide (R true and explains A)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', oxides and oxoanions of metals
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Applying Hund's rule to the free (gaseous) ions, how many of the following have the same number of unpaired electrons, and hence the same spin-only magnetic moment, as Fe²⁺?
Ti²⁺, Cr²⁺, Mn³⁺, Fe³⁺, Co³⁺, Ni²⁺
(Atomic numbers: Ti 22, Cr 24, Mn 25, Fe 26, Co 27, Ni 28)

solution.concept: Unpaired electrons from the d-electron count
solution.explanation: Fe²⁺ is 3d⁶ with four unpaired electrons. A d⁴ ion (four singly occupied orbitals) and another d⁶ ion also have four unpaired electrons.
steps: Same as Fe²⁺: Cr²⁺, Mn³⁺, Co³⁺ → 3
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 misses Co³⁺, which is isoelectronic with Fe²⁺. 4 wrongly adds Fe³⁺ (five unpaired). 5 also adds both d² and d⁸ ions, which have only two unpaired electrons.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', magnetic properties

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The IUPAC name of [Cr(NH₃)₃(H₂O)₃]Cl₃ is:

solution.explanation: Ligands are named in alphabetical order (ammine before aqua; the prefix tri is ignored). The complex is a cation, so the metal keeps its ordinary name, followed by its oxidation state.
solution.why_others_wrong: Triaquatriammine breaks the alphabetical order. 'Chromate' is used only for an anionic complex. (II) gives the wrong oxidation state.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', nomenclature of coordination compounds

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match the coordination entity in List-I with the oxidation state of its central metal in List-II.

List-I:
A. [Ni(CO)₄]
B. [Ag(CN)₂]⁻
C. [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺
D. [PtCl₆]²⁻

List-II:
I. +2
II. 0
III. +4
IV. +1

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Oxidation number of the central atom
solution.explanation: Oxidation number = charge on the entity − total charge of the ligands. CO and NH₃ are neutral; CN⁻ and Cl⁻ carry −1 each.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-IV, B-II swaps nickel and silver. B-I, C-IV gives silver +2 and copper +1. C-III, D-I gives copper +4 and platinum +2, ignoring the six chloride ligands.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', definitions (oxidation number of central atom)
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The formula of tetraamminecopper(II) sulphate is:

solution.concept: Writing a formula from the name
solution.explanation: The name gives a complex cation with four ammine ligands and Cu(II), so the cation is [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺. One sulphate ion (2−) balances it.
solution.why_others_wrong: (SO₄)₂ would need copper(IV). [Cu(SO₄)(NH₃)₄] puts sulphate inside the coordination sphere, which the name (no 'sulphato') does not say. [Cu(NH₃)₂]SO₄ has only two ammine ligands.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', formulas of mononuclear coordination entities

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Optical isomers (enantiomers) are mirror images of each other that cannot be superimposed on one another.
Statement II: Optical isomerism is common in octahedral complexes containing didentate ligands.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT defines optical isomers as non-superimposable mirror images and notes that optical isomerism is common in octahedral complexes involving didentate ligands, such as [Co(en)₃]³⁺.
steps: Statement I: definition of enantiomers → true
Statement II: e.g. [Co(en)₃]³⁺ and cis-[PtCl₂(en)₂]²⁺ are chiral → true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', isomerism (optical isomerism)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): One mole of [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃ gives three moles of AgCl when treated with excess AgNO₃ solution.
Reason (R): NH₃ is a stronger field ligand than H₂O.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: All three chlorides of [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃ lie outside the coordination sphere and are free Cl⁻ ions, so they are precipitated as 3AgCl. The position of NH₃ in the spectrochemical series is true but concerns crystal field splitting; it has nothing to do with how many chlorides are ionisable.
steps: NH₃ > H₂O in the spectrochemical series (R true)
R explains splitting, not the number of ionisable Cl⁻ → R is not the explanation
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', Werner's theory; crystal field theory (spectrochemical series)
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: [Mn(CN)₆]³⁻ is a low-spin octahedral complex (Z of Mn = 25). Its spin-only magnetic moment is about:

solution.explanation: Mn³⁺ is 3d⁴. CN⁻ is a strong field ligand (Δo > P), so all four electrons go into the t₂g set: t₂g⁴ eg⁰. Three orbitals hold four electrons, so one pair forms and two electrons stay unpaired.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.90 BM is the high-spin value (t₂g³ eg¹, four unpaired). 3.87 BM assumes three unpaired electrons, and 1.73 BM only one; neither fits t₂g⁴.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', crystal field splitting in octahedral complexes

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: An octahedral complex of the type [MA₃B₃] can exist as facial (fac) and meridional (mer) isomers.
Statement II: In the mer isomer, the three identical ligands occupy the three corners of one face of the octahedron.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: In the fac isomer the three donor atoms of the same ligand sit at the corners of one octahedral face; in the mer isomer they lie around a meridian of the octahedron. Statement II describes the fac isomer.
steps: Statement I: [Co(NH₃)₃(NO₂)₃] has fac and mer forms → true
Statement II: 'corners of one face' = fac, not mer → false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', geometrical isomerism (fac and mer)
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The IUPAC name of [CoCl₂(en)₂]Cl (en = ethane-1,2-diamine) is:

solution.concept: Naming a complex with a polydentate ligand
solution.explanation: Ligands are taken alphabetically by their names (chlorido before ethane-1,2-diamine); multiplying prefixes are ignored. For a ligand whose name already contains a numeral, bis/tris is used and the name is put in brackets. The complex is a cation, so the metal is 'cobalt'.
solution.why_others_wrong: Putting bis(ethane-1,2-diamine) first breaks the alphabetical order. Cobalt(II) ignores the two chlorido ligands in the charge. 'di' cannot be used before a bracketed ligand name, and 'cobaltate' is only for anionic complexes.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', nomenclature of coordination compounds

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about crystal field splitting and colour are correct?

(a) In a free (isolated) metal ion, the five d orbitals are degenerate.
(b) [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is colourless because Ni²⁺ has no unpaired electrons.
(c) When ethane-1,2-diamine is added gradually to a solution of [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺, the colour changes, because en is a stronger field ligand than H₂O.
(d) A complex with a larger Δo absorbs light of longer wavelength.
(e) Ruby is aluminium oxide containing a small percentage of Cr³⁺ ions.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Crystal field theory and the colour of complexes
solution.explanation: The d orbitals are degenerate only in the free ion. [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (d⁸, two unpaired electrons) is green; replacing H₂O by the stronger field en increases Δo and changes the colour. A larger Δo means absorption of higher energy, i.e. shorter wavelength. Ruby is Al₂O₃ with about 0.5–1% Cr³⁺ (d³) ions in octahedral sites.
steps: (a) degenerate d orbitals in a free ion → true
(b) Ni²⁺ is d⁸ with two unpaired e⁻; the ion is green → false
(c) stronger ligand → larger Δo → new colour → true
(d) larger Δo → shorter λ absorbed → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Every other option includes (b) or (d), both false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', crystal field theory (colour in coordination compounds)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ is an inner orbital complex.
Reason (R): In [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺, cobalt uses its inner 3d orbitals in d²sp³ hybridisation.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Co³⁺ is 3d⁶. With NH₃, the six electrons pair up in three 3d orbitals, freeing two inner 3d orbitals, so the metal uses 3d, 4s and 4p orbitals (d²sp³). A complex that uses inner (n−1)d orbitals is called an inner orbital (low spin) complex, which is exactly what R says.
steps: (n−1)d used → inner orbital complex; R gives the reason
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', valence bond theory
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In [Ni(NH₃)₆]²⁺ (Z of Ni = 28), the hybridisation of nickel and the magnetic behaviour of the complex are:

options.text: d²sp³, paramagnetic with two unpaired electrons
sp³d², paramagnetic with two unpaired electrons

solution.concept: Outer orbital octahedral complex of a d⁸ ion
solution.explanation: Ni²⁺ is 3d⁸. Even if electrons pair, eight electrons fill four of the five 3d orbitals, leaving only one vacant 3d orbital; two are needed for d²sp³. So the octahedral complex uses 4s, 4p and two 4d orbitals (sp³d²), and the two unpaired 3d electrons remain.
steps: Two vacant inner d orbitals are not available → outer orbital sp³d²
solution.why_others_wrong: d²sp³ would need two empty 3d orbitals, impossible for d⁸. Any 'diamagnetic' option ignores the two unpaired 3d electrons that every octahedral Ni²⁺ complex keeps.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', valence bond theory (outer orbital complexes)
solution.final_answer: Option D: sp³d², paramagnetic with two unpaired electrons

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In black-and-white photography, the developed film is fixed by washing with hypo (sodium thiosulphate) solution, which dissolves the undecomposed silver bromide. The complex ion formed is:

solution.concept: Use of complex formation in photography
solution.explanation: AgBr dissolves in hypo because Ag⁺ forms the soluble complex [Ag(S₂O₃)₂]³⁻.
steps: Ag(+1) with two S₂O₃²⁻ → overall charge 1 − 4 = −3
solution.why_others_wrong: [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ forms with ammonia and [Ag(CN)₂]⁻ with cyanide, neither of which is hypo. [Ag(S₂O₃)]⁺ has the wrong charge (+1 − 2 = −1) and the wrong number of ligands.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', importance and applications of coordination compounds

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
How many of the following are inner orbital (d²sp³) complexes according to valence bond theory?
[Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺, [CoF₆]³⁻, [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻, [FeF₆]³⁻, [Cr(NH₃)₆]³⁺, [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺
(Atomic numbers: Cr 24, Fe 26, Co 27)

solution.concept: Inner versus outer orbital octahedral complexes
solution.explanation: Strong field ligands (NH₃ with Co³⁺, CN⁻) pair the d electrons and free two 3d orbitals (d²sp³). F⁻ and H₂O with Fe or Co leave the electrons unpaired, so 4d orbitals are used (sp³d²). Cr³⁺ is d³, so two 3d orbitals are empty anyway and the complex is always d²sp³.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 leaves out [Cr(NH₃)₆]³⁺, forgetting that a d³ ion always has two vacant 3d orbitals. 4 or 5 counts one or more of the high-spin fluoro or aqua complexes as inner orbital.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', valence bond theory

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about metal carbonyls are correct?

(a) [Ni(CO)₄] is tetrahedral.
(b) [Fe(CO)₅] is trigonal bipyramidal.
(c) [Cr(CO)₆] is octahedral.
(d) The σ bond in a metal carbonyl is formed by donation of a lone pair on the oxygen atom of CO to the metal.
(e) The synergic effect of σ donation and π back-donation strengthens the bond between CO and the metal.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Structure and bonding of metal carbonyls
solution.explanation: NCERT gives the shapes: tetrahedral Ni(CO)₄, trigonal bipyramidal Fe(CO)₅, octahedral Cr(CO)₆. The M–C σ bond uses the lone pair on the carbon of CO; π back-donation from a filled metal d orbital into the vacant π* orbital of CO creates a synergic effect that strengthens the M–CO bond.
steps: (d) the donor atom is carbon, not oxygen → false
(e) synergic σ/π bonding strengthens the bond → true
solution.why_others_wrong: (a), (b), (c) only and (b), (c), (e) only each leave out a true statement; the option with (d) includes a false one.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', bonding in metal carbonyls

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): [Mn(H₂O)₆]²⁺ has a low-spin configuration with only one unpaired electron.
Reason (R): With H₂O as the ligand, the crystal field splitting Δo for Mn²⁺ is smaller than the pairing energy P.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Mn²⁺ is 3d⁵. Because Δo < P for the aqua complex, the electrons occupy the eg orbitals rather than pair: t₂g³ eg², with five unpaired electrons (high spin). So A is false while R is true.
steps: Δo < P → t₂g³ eg² → five unpaired electrons (high spin)
A (low spin, one unpaired) → false; R → true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', crystal field splitting (Δo and pairing energy)
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match the complex in List-I with its spin-only magnetic moment in List-II (atomic numbers: Cr 24, Mn 25, Fe 26, Cu 29; [MnCl₄]²⁻ is tetrahedral).

List-I:
A. [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺
B. [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻
C. [MnCl₄]²⁻
D. [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺

List-II:
I. 0 BM
II. 1.73 BM
III. 3.87 BM
IV. 5.92 BM

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Unpaired electrons from d count and ligand field
solution.explanation: Count the d electrons, decide whether pairing occurs, then use μ = √[n(n + 2)].
steps: Fe²⁺ d⁶ with CN⁻ (strong) → t₂g⁶, n = 0 → 0 (I)
Mn²⁺ d⁵ with Cl⁻ in a tetrahedral field (small Δt) → n = 5 → 5.92 BM (IV)
Cu²⁺ d⁹ → n = 1 in any geometry → 1.73 BM (II)
solution.why_others_wrong: A-IV, C-III swaps chromium and manganese. B-II, D-I gives Cu²⁺ zero unpaired electrons, but a d⁹ ion always has one. A-II, D-III swaps the Cr³⁺ and Cu²⁺ values.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', crystal field theory; magnetic properties
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Purification and Characterisation of Organic Compounds
questions.question_text: In Lassaigne's test, the sodium fusion extract is acidified with nitric acid and treated with silver nitrate. A yellow precipitate that is insoluble in ammonium hydroxide is obtained. The halogen present is:

solution.explanation: NCERT: a white precipitate soluble in NH₄OH shows chlorine; a yellowish precipitate sparingly soluble in NH₄OH shows bromine; a yellow precipitate insoluble in NH₄OH shows iodine.
steps: AgCl white, soluble in NH₄OH; AgBr pale yellow, sparingly soluble
AgI yellow, insoluble in NH₄OH → iodine
solution.why_others_wrong: AgCl is white and dissolves in ammonia; AgBr is pale yellow and dissolves partly. AgF is soluble in water, so fluoride gives no precipitate.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', detection of halogens

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Purification and Characterisation of Organic Compounds
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): During crystallisation, coloured impurities are removed by adsorbing them on activated charcoal.
Reason (R): Repeated crystallisation is needed when the compound and its impurities have comparable solubilities.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Both are NCERT statements about crystallisation, but they deal with different problems. Charcoal removes impurities that colour the solution by adsorption; repeated crystallisation is about separating substances of similar solubility. R does not explain why charcoal is used.
steps: A: activated charcoal adsorbs coloured impurities → true
R: comparable solubilities → repeated crystallisation → true
R concerns solubility, not colour → not the explanation
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', crystallisation
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Purification and Characterisation of Organic Compounds
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Differential extraction is carried out in a separating funnel, using an organic solvent that is immiscible with water.
Statement II: The name chromatography comes from the Greek word chroma (colour), because the technique was first used to separate coloured substances found in plants.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: In differential extraction, the aqueous solution is shaken with an immiscible organic solvent in a separating funnel, and the two layers are separated. NCERT explains that 'chromatography' comes from 'chroma', since it was first used to separate coloured plant pigments.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', differential extraction; chromatography
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Purification and Characterisation of Organic Compounds
questions.question_text: Aniline is purified by steam distillation at an atmospheric pressure of 760 mm Hg. At the temperature at which the mixture distils, the vapour pressure of water is 717 mm Hg. The vapour pressure of aniline at this temperature is:

solution.explanation: A mixture of steam and the organic liquid boils when the sum of the vapour pressures of the organic liquid (p₁) and water (p₂) equals the atmospheric pressure: p = p₁ + p₂. Each liquid therefore boils below its normal boiling point.
solution.why_others_wrong: 717 mm Hg is the vapour pressure of water, not aniline. 760 mm Hg assumes aniline alone must reach atmospheric pressure, as in simple distillation. 1477 mm Hg adds instead of subtracting.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', steam distillation

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Purification and Characterisation of Organic Compounds
questions.question_text:
After a thin layer chromatography (TLC) run, the spots have to be located. Match the kind of compound in List-I with the way its spots are made visible in List-II.

List-I:
A. Coloured compounds
B. Amino acids
C. Colourless compounds that fluoresce
D. Colourless compounds that adsorb iodine

List-II:
I. Spraying the plate with ninhydrin solution
II. Seen directly on the plate
III. Keeping the plate in a closed jar containing a few iodine crystals
IV. Viewing the plate under ultraviolet light

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Detecting spots in thin layer chromatography
solution.explanation: NCERT lists the ways of locating spots: coloured compounds are visible by their own colour; fluorescing compounds show under UV light; compounds that adsorb iodine show brown spots in an iodine jar; amino acids are detected by spraying ninhydrin.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-I, B-II swaps the coloured compounds and amino acids. C-III, D-IV swaps UV light and the iodine jar. B-IV, C-I gives ninhydrin to the fluorescent compounds.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', thin layer chromatography
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Purification and Characterisation of Organic Compounds
questions.question_text: A hydrocarbon contains 92.3% carbon and 7.7% hydrogen by mass. Its vapour density is 39. The molecular formula of the hydrocarbon is (C = 12, H = 1):

solution.concept: Empirical and molecular formula from percentage composition
solution.explanation: Find the mole ratio of the elements, then use molar mass = 2 × vapour density to find the multiple of the empirical formula.
steps: C: 92.3/12 = 7.69; H: 7.7/1 = 7.7 → ratio 1 : 1 → empirical formula CH (13 g mol⁻¹)
solution.why_others_wrong: C₃H₃ uses the vapour density itself as the molar mass. C₁₂H₁₂ multiplies the vapour density by 4. CH is the empirical formula, not the molecular formula.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry', empirical and molecular formulae; Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', quantitative analysis

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Purification and Characterisation of Organic Compounds
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the detection of elements in organic compounds are correct?

(a) When the compound is heated with copper(II) oxide, its carbon is oxidised to CO₂, which turns lime water milky.
(b) In the same test, hydrogen is oxidised to water, which turns anhydrous copper sulphate blue.
(c) Phosphorus is oxidised to phosphate, which gives a yellow colour or precipitate with ammonium molybdate after boiling with nitric acid.
(d) During sodium fusion, sulphur in the compound is converted into sodium sulphate.
(e) In the copper(II) oxide test, carbon is converted into carbon monoxide.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Detection of C, H, S and P
solution.explanation: Carbon becomes CO₂ (lime water turns milky) and hydrogen becomes water (white anhydrous CuSO₄ turns blue). Phosphorus is oxidised (e.g. with sodium peroxide) to phosphate, which gives a yellow colour or precipitate with ammonium molybdate. In sodium fusion, sulphur forms sodium sulphide, Na₂S, not sulphate.
steps: (a) C → CO₂ → lime water milky → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Every other option contains (d) or (e), or leaves out the true statement (c) or (a).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', qualitative analysis

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text: The IUPAC name of (CH₃)₂CH–CH₂–CH(CH₃)₂ is:

solution.explanation: The longest chain has five carbons, with a methyl group on C-2 and on C-4 (the numbering is the same from either end).
steps: Methyl groups at C-2 and C-4
solution.why_others_wrong: 2,2- and 3,3-dimethylpentane put both methyls on one carbon, which is a different compound. 1,1,3-Trimethylbutane does not use the longest chain (a methyl on C-1 extends it).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', IUPAC nomenclature of alkanes

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text: How many structural isomers have the molecular formula C₅H₁₂?

solution.explanation: C₅H₁₂ can have a straight chain of five carbons, a four-carbon chain with one methyl branch, or a three-carbon chain with two methyl branches on the middle carbon.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 or 5 counts the same skeleton twice (for example 3-methylbutane is 2-methylbutane numbered from the wrong end). 2 misses neopentane.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', structural isomerism

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Pentan-2-one and pentan-3-one are position isomers.
Statement II: Butane and 2-methylpropane are position isomers.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Pentan-2-one and pentan-3-one have the same carbon chain and differ only in the position of the C=O group. Butane and 2-methylpropane differ in the carbon skeleton itself, which is chain isomerism.
steps: Statement I: same chain, C=O at C-2 or C-3 → position isomers → true
Statement II: straight vs branched chain → chain isomers, not position isomers → false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', structural isomerism
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Ethanol and methoxymethane are chain isomers.
Reason (R): Ethanol and methoxymethane have the same molecular formula but different functional groups.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Ethanol (C₂H₅OH) and methoxymethane (CH₃OCH₃) are both C₂H₆O, but one is an alcohol and the other an ether. Isomers that differ in functional group are functional group isomers, not chain isomers.
steps: Alcohol vs ether → functional group isomers
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', functional group isomerism
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match the class of compound in List-I with the suffix used for it in IUPAC names in List-II.

List-I:
A. Alcohol
B. Aldehyde
C. Ketone
D. Carboxylic acid

List-II:
I. -oic acid
II. -one
III. -al
IV. -ol

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: When a functional group is the principal group, its suffix replaces the final 'e' of the alkane name.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-III, B-IV swaps alcohol and aldehyde. B-II, C-III swaps aldehyde and ketone. C-I, D-II swaps ketone and acid.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', nomenclature of compounds with functional groups
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text:
How many of the following show geometrical (cis–trans) isomerism?
But-2-ene, propene, 2-methylbut-2-ene, pent-2-ene, 1,2-dichloroethene, 1,1-dichloroethene

solution.explanation: An alkene shows cis–trans isomerism only if each doubly bonded carbon carries two different groups.
steps: But-2-ene: CH₃/H on both carbons → yes
Propene: =CH₂ end has H, H → no
2-Methylbut-2-ene: one carbon has CH₃, CH₃ → no
1,1-Dichloroethene: one carbon has H, H → no
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 misses one of the qualifying alkenes (often 1,2-dichloroethene, which has no alkyl group). 4 or 5 includes a compound with two identical groups on one double-bond carbon.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', isomerism in alkenes (geometrical isomerism)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text: The IUPAC name of CH₃–CH₂–CH(CH₂CH₃)–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃ is:

solution.explanation: The longest chain has six carbons (through the propyl side), with an ethyl group on the third carbon when numbered from the end nearer the branch.
steps: Substituent: ethyl; numbering from the left gives locant 3 (from the right, 4)
solution.why_others_wrong: 3-Propylpentane uses a five-carbon chain, not the longest. 4-Ethylhexane numbers from the wrong end. 2-Ethylhexane is never correct: an ethyl on C-2 would lengthen the main chain.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', IUPAC nomenclature (branched chain alkanes)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In but-2-ene, CH₃–CH=CH–CH₃, all four carbon atoms are sp² hybridised.
Reason (R): A carbon atom that forms a carbon–carbon double bond is sp² hybridised.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Only C-2 and C-3, which form the double bond, are sp². The two terminal CH₃ carbons form four single bonds and are sp³.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', shapes of carbon compounds (hybridisation)
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about isomerism are correct?

(a) Metamerism arises from different alkyl chains on either side of the functional group in the molecule.
(b) But-1-ene and but-2-ene are position isomers.
(c) Propanoic acid and methyl ethanoate are functional group isomers.
(d) Stereoisomers differ in the sequence in which the atoms are bonded to one another.
(e) Structural isomers have the same structural formula but different arrangements of atoms in space.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Metamers (e.g. C₂H₅OC₂H₅ and CH₃OC₃H₇) differ in the alkyl groups on either side of the functional group. But-1-ene and but-2-ene differ in the position of the double bond. Propanoic acid and methyl ethanoate are both C₃H₆O₂ but an acid and an ester. Structural isomers differ in the sequence of bonding; stereoisomers have the same sequence but differ in the spatial arrangement — (d) and (e) swap these definitions.
steps: (c) acid vs ester, both C₃H₆O₂ → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Every other option contains (d) or (e), or leaves out a true statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', isomerism

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The IUPAC name of CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CHO is butan-1-al.
Statement II: The IUPAC name of CH₃–CH₂–COCl is propanoyl chloride.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: The –CHO carbon of an aldehyde is always C-1, so no locant is written: the name is butanal. An acid chloride is named by replacing '-oic acid' with '-oyl chloride': propanoic acid → propanoyl chloride.
steps: Statement I: correct name is butanal → false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', nomenclature of compounds with functional groups
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text: How many aromatic compounds (containing a benzene ring) have the molecular formula C₈H₁₀?

solution.concept: Structural isomers of a substituted benzene
solution.explanation: C₈H₁₀ with a benzene ring is C₆H₄(CH₃)₂ or C₆H₅C₂H₅. The two methyl groups can be ortho, meta or para.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 counts only the three xylenes and misses ethylbenzene. 5 or 6 counts the same dimethylbenzene twice (e.g. 1,5- is the same as 1,3-).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', isomerism; Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', nomenclature and isomerism of aromatic hydrocarbons

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match the electronic effect in List-I with its description in List-II.

List-I:
A. Inductive effect
B. Resonance effect
C. Electromeric effect
D. Hyperconjugation

List-II:
I. Temporary complete shift of a shared π pair to one atom, only in the presence of an attacking reagent
II. Delocalisation of the σ electrons of a C–H bond of an alkyl group into an adjacent empty p orbital or π system
III. Permanent polarisation transmitted along a chain of σ bonds
IV. Permanent delocalisation of π electrons (or lone pairs) in a conjugated system

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: The inductive and resonance effects are permanent; the electromeric effect is temporary and needs an attacking reagent; hyperconjugation involves σ (C–H) electrons.
steps: Resonance → π / lone pair, conjugated system → IV
solution.why_others_wrong: A-IV, B-III swaps the inductive and resonance effects. B-II, D-IV swaps resonance and hyperconjugation. C-II, D-I swaps the electromeric effect and hyperconjugation.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', electron movement in organic reactions (electronic effects)
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text: How many structural isomers (open-chain and cyclic together) have the molecular formula C₄H₈? Count cis and trans forms as one structure.

solution.concept: Isomers of CₙH₂ₙ: alkenes and cycloalkanes
solution.explanation: CₙH₂ₙ fits both alkenes and cycloalkanes, so ring isomers must be counted as well as open-chain alkenes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 counts only the open-chain alkenes. 4 misses methylcyclopropane. 6 counts cis- and trans-but-2-ene separately, which the question excludes.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', structural isomerism; Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', isomerism in alkenes

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about hyperconjugation are correct?

(a) Hyperconjugation is a permanent effect.
(b) The tert-butyl cation has fewer C–H bonds able to take part in hyperconjugation than the ethyl cation.
(c) Hyperconjugation is also called no-bond resonance.
(d) The greater the number of alkyl groups attached to the positively charged carbon, the greater the hyperconjugation and the more stable the carbocation.
(e) Hyperconjugation is the overlap of the π electrons of a C=C bond with an empty p orbital.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Hyperconjugation is the permanent delocalisation of σ electrons of a C–H bond of an alkyl group attached to an atom with an unshared p orbital or to an unsaturated system; it is also called no-bond resonance. (CH₃)₃C⁺ has nine such C–H bonds and CH₃CH₂⁺ only three, so the tert-butyl cation is more stable.
steps: (b) 9 vs 3 C–H bonds — tert-butyl has more → false
(d) more alkyl groups → more stable cation → true
(e) delocalisation of π electrons is resonance, not hyperconjugation → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Every other option includes (b) or (e), which are false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', hyperconjugation

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Heterolytic cleavage of the C–Br bond in (CH₃)₃C–Br gives (CH₃)₃C⁺ and Br⁻.
Reason (R): Carbon is more electronegative than bromine.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: In heterolysis, the shared pair goes to the more electronegative atom. Bromine is more electronegative than carbon, so it leaves as Br⁻ and the tertiary carbon becomes a carbocation.
steps: Br more electronegative than C → takes the bond pair
R reverses the electronegativity order → false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', fission of a covalent bond
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The canonical (resonance) structures of a molecule must have the same number of unpaired electrons.
Statement II: Among the canonical structures, one with a negative charge on the more electronegative atom contributes more to the resonance hybrid.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: canonical structures have the same positions of nuclei and the same number of unpaired electrons. More stable structures — more covalent bonds, octets on all atoms, less separation of opposite charges, a negative charge on the more electronegative atom — contribute more.
steps: Statement I: same number of unpaired electrons → true
Statement II: negative charge on the more electronegative atom → more stable → larger contribution → true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', resonance structure
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text: The IUPAC name of HOOC–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–CHO is:

solution.concept: Polyfunctional compounds: principal group and locants
solution.explanation: The carboxylic acid group ranks above the aldehyde, so it is the principal group (suffix -oic acid) and its carbon is C-1. The aldehyde carbon, lying in the chain, is named with the prefix 'oxo'.
steps: C-2 = CH₂, C-3 = CH(CH₃), C-4 = CHO
solution.why_others_wrong: 2-Methyl misplaces the methyl group, which is on C-3 counted from the COOH carbon. 3-Carboxy-2-methylpropanal treats the aldehyde as the principal group although –COOH ranks higher. 3-Methylbutanoic acid leaves out the oxo group (it names a different compound).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', nomenclature of polyfunctional compounds

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Higher alkanes, on heating to a high temperature, decompose into lower alkanes, alkenes and so on. This decomposition is called:

solution.explanation: NCERT: breaking of larger alkanes into smaller fragments by the application of heat is pyrolysis or cracking, e.g. dodecane gives heptane and pentene.
steps: Heat → C–C bonds break → smaller alkanes and alkenes
solution.why_others_wrong: Isomerisation rearranges a chain without breaking it into smaller molecules. Aromatisation converts n-alkanes (C6 or more) into benzene homologues. Combustion needs oxygen and gives CO₂ and water.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', alkanes (pyrolysis)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 2.8 g of ethene reacts completely with bromine dissolved in CCl₄. The mass of 1,2-dibromoethane formed is (C = 12, H = 1, Br = 80):

solution.concept: Addition of bromine to an alkene
solution.explanation: One mole of ethene adds one mole of Br₂ to give one mole of CH₂Br–CH₂Br.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9.4 g uses only one bromine atom per molecule (or halves the answer). 37.6 g doubles it. 16.0 g is the mass of bromine consumed, not of the product.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', alkenes (addition of halogens)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Alkanes are also called paraffins, because they have little affinity for (are unreactive towards) most reagents.
Statement II: In alkanes each carbon atom is sp³ hybridised; the C–C and C–H bond lengths are 154 pm and 112 pm respectively.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: 'Paraffin' comes from parum affinis (little affinity). NCERT gives the C–C and C–H bond lengths in alkanes as 154 pm and 112 pm, with sp³ carbons.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', alkanes
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The mass of carbon dioxide formed by the complete combustion of 4.2 g of propene is (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16):

solution.explanation: C₃H₆ + 9/2 O₂ → 3CO₂ + 3H₂O: each mole of propene gives three moles of CO₂.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.4 g and 8.8 g take one or two CO₂ per propene. 5.4 g is the mass of water formed.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', combustion of hydrocarbons

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 1.4 g of an open-chain alkene adds exactly 4.0 g of bromine. The molecular formula of the alkene is (C = 12, H = 1, Br = 80):

solution.explanation: An alkene has one C=C bond and adds one Br₂ (160 g mol⁻¹) per molecule.
solution.why_others_wrong: C₂H₄ uses 80 g mol⁻¹ (atomic Br) for bromine. C₈H₁₆ assumes two Br₂ per molecule, which an alkene with one double bond cannot add. C₄H₆ is not an alkene formula (CₙH₂ₙ₋₂).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', alkenes (addition of halogens)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 9.2 g of ethanol is heated with excess concentrated sulphuric acid at 443 K and is converted completely into ethene. The volume of ethene at STP is (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16; molar volume at STP = 22.4 L mol⁻¹):

solution.concept: Preparation of alkenes by acidic dehydration of alcohols
solution.explanation: C₂H₅OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O (conc. H₂SO₄, 443 K): one mole of ethanol gives one mole of ethene.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.24 L halves the amount (as if two ethanol gave one ethene, which is ether formation). 8.96 L doubles it. 1.12 L divides by four.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', preparation of alkenes (acidic dehydration of alcohols)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which of the following reacts with sodamide (NaNH₂) to form a sodium salt, showing that it has an acidic hydrogen?

solution.explanation: A hydrogen attached to a triply bonded (sp, 50% s character) carbon is weakly acidic and can be removed by strong bases such as NaNH₂. Only a terminal alkyne has such a hydrogen.
steps: But-1-yne: HC≡C–CH₂CH₃ has an ≡C–H → CH₃CH₂C≡C⁻Na⁺ + NH₃
Alkene and alkane hydrogens are not acidic enough
solution.why_others_wrong: But-2-yne is an internal alkyne with no hydrogen on an sp carbon. The sp² (alkene) and sp³ (alkane) C–H bonds are far less acidic and do not react with sodamide.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', alkynes (acidic character of alkyne)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match the substituent on a benzene ring in List-I with its effect on electrophilic substitution in List-II.

List-I:
A. –OH
B. –NO₂
C. –Cl
D. –CH₃

List-II:
I. Activating and ortho/para-directing, mainly through the +R effect
II. Activating and ortho/para-directing, through the +I effect and hyperconjugation
III. Deactivating but ortho/para-directing
IV. Deactivating and meta-directing

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: –OH donates a lone pair into the ring (+R). –CH₃ donates through +I and hyperconjugation. –Cl withdraws by −I more than it donates by +R, so it deactivates, but its +R effect still directs to ortho/para. –NO₂ withdraws by −I and −R and directs to meta.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-II, D-I swaps the mechanisms of –OH and –CH₃. B-III, C-IV swaps the nitro group and chlorine. C-II, D-III makes chlorine activating and the methyl group deactivating.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', directive influence of a functional group in monosubstituted benzene
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-I, B-IV, C-III, D-II

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the physical and chemical properties of alkanes are correct?

(a) The first four members, C₁ to C₄, are gases at 298 K.
(b) Alkanes from C₅ to C₁₇ are liquids at 298 K.
(c) The boiling points of straight-chain alkanes rise as the molecular mass increases.
(d) Alkanes dissolve readily in water.
(e) Alkanes readily undergo addition reactions.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: C₁–C₄ are gases, C₅–C₁₇ liquids and C₁₈ onwards solids at 298 K; boiling points rise with molecular mass because van der Waals forces increase. Alkanes are non-polar, so they are insoluble in water, and being saturated they give substitution, not addition, reactions.
solution.why_others_wrong: Every other option includes (d) or (e), both false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', alkanes (physical and chemical properties)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In the second step of electrophilic substitution in benzene, the arenium ion (σ-complex) loses a proton.
Reason (R): Loss of the proton restores the aromatic character of the ring.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Attack of the electrophile forms an arenium ion in which one carbon is sp³ and aromaticity is lost. The ion then loses H⁺ from that sp³ carbon (removed by, e.g., AlCl₄⁻ or HSO₄⁻), which regenerates the aromatic sextet. Regaining aromatic stability is why a proton is lost instead of a nucleophile being added.
steps: Step 2: loss of H⁺ → aromatic ring restored
R gives the driving force for A → R explains A
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', mechanism of electrophilic substitution reactions
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 20 mL of a mixture of methane and ethene is burnt completely in excess oxygen. The carbon dioxide formed measures 32 mL, all volumes being measured at the same temperature and pressure. The percentage of ethene by volume in the mixture is:

solution.concept: Gas volume stoichiometry for a mixture
solution.explanation: CH₄ gives 1 volume of CO₂ per volume and C₂H₄ gives 2 volumes of CO₂ per volume (Avogadro's law).
steps: Let CH₄ = x mL, C₂H₄ = (20 − x) mL
solution.why_others_wrong: 40% is the percentage of methane. 80% assigns all the CO₂ to ethene (32/2 = 16 mL). 50% assumes an equal mixture without solving.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', combustion; Class 11 Chemistry, 'Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry', stoichiometry

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the preparation and reactions of alkenes are correct?

(a) The ease of dehydration of alcohols by concentrated sulphuric acid follows the order tertiary > secondary > primary.
(b) Ozonolysis of ethene (O₃, then Zn/H₂O) gives two molecules of methanal.
(c) The presence of a peroxide changes the product of the addition of HBr to but-2-ene.
(d) Acidified KMnO₄ oxidises 2-methylpropene to propanone, carbon dioxide and water.
(e) Ethene adds bromine in CCl₄ to give 1,1-dibromoethane.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Tertiary alcohols dehydrate most easily because their carbocations are most stable. Ozonolysis splits CH₂=CH₂ into two HCHO. But-2-ene is symmetrical, so HBr gives 2-bromobutane with or without peroxide. Acidic permanganate cleaves (CH₃)₂C=CH₂ into (CH₃)₂C=O and CO₂ + H₂O. Br₂ adds across the double bond, one Br on each carbon (1,2-dibromoethane).
solution.why_others_wrong: Each other option includes (c) or (e), or leaves out (d) or (a).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', alkenes (preparation and chemical properties); Class 12 Chemistry, 'Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers', dehydration

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Benzene is more stable than the hypothetical cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene with localised double bonds.
Reason (R): Benzene contains alternating C–C single and C=C double bonds of different lengths.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: The six π electrons of benzene are delocalised, which lowers its energy (resonance stabilisation). As a result, all six C–C bonds have the same length, 139 pm, between the C–C (154 pm) and C=C (134 pm) values; there are no separate single and double bonds.
steps: R: all C–C bonds equal (139 pm) → false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', structure of benzene (resonance and stability)
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Propene is treated with HBr in the presence of benzoyl peroxide to give X. X is heated with sodium in dry ether to give Y. Y is:

solution.concept: Anti-Markovnikov addition followed by Wurtz coupling
solution.explanation: With peroxide, HBr adds to propene against Markovnikov's rule to give 1-bromopropane (X). The Wurtz reaction joins two propyl groups end to end: CH₃CH₂CH₂–CH₂CH₂CH₃.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2,3-Dimethylbutane would come from 2-bromopropane, the product without peroxide. 2-Methylpentane would need a mixed n-propyl/isopropyl coupling. Propane would need reduction of X, not the Wurtz reaction.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', peroxide effect; Wurtz reaction

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A compound that rotates the plane of plane-polarised light in the clockwise direction is called:

solution.explanation: NCERT: a compound that rotates the plane of polarised light to the right (clockwise) is dextrorotatory, shown by (+) or d; one that rotates it anticlockwise is laevorotatory, (−) or l.
solution.why_others_wrong: Laevorotatory compounds rotate the plane anticlockwise. A racemic mixture shows zero rotation because the two enantiomers cancel. An achiral compound is optically inactive.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Haloalkanes and Haloarenes', stereochemical aspects (optical activity)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane is hydrolysed by aqueous alkali by the SN1 mechanism. At the same temperature, the concentration of the alkyl bromide is doubled and that of OH⁻ is tripled. The rate of reaction increases by a factor of:

solution.concept: Rate law of an SN1 reaction
solution.explanation: In SN1, the slow step is the ionisation of the alkyl halide to a carbocation, so rate = k[RX]; the nucleophile does not appear in the rate law.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 uses the SN2 rate law, k[RX][OH⁻]. 3 makes the rate depend on OH⁻ only. 1 ignores the change in the alkyl halide concentration.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Haloalkanes and Haloarenes', nucleophilic substitution (SN1 mechanism)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In haloalkanes, the carbon–halogen bond is polar, with a partial positive charge on carbon.
Statement II: The carbon–halogen bond enthalpy decreases in the order C–F > C–Cl > C–Br > C–I.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Halogens are more electronegative than carbon, so the C–X bond is polarised Cδ⁺–Xδ⁻. As the halogen atom becomes larger, the C–X bond becomes longer and weaker, so its bond enthalpy falls from C–F to C–I.
steps: Statement II → true (bond length rises, bond enthalpy falls)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Haloalkanes and Haloarenes', nature of C–X bond
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 9.5 g of bromomethane is heated with silver fluoride and converted completely into fluoromethane (Swarts reaction). The mass of fluoromethane formed is (C = 12, H = 1, F = 19, Br = 80):

solution.explanation: CH₃Br + AgF → CH₃F + AgBr: one mole of bromomethane gives one mole of fluoromethane.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.9 g is the mass of fluorine alone. 6.8 g doubles the amount. 9.5 g assumes the mass does not change.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Haloalkanes and Haloarenes', halogen exchange (Swarts reaction)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match the stereochemical term in List-I with its description in List-II.

List-I:
A. Retention
B. Inversion
C. Racemisation
D. Enantiomers

List-II:
I. Conversion of an optically active compound into a 50 : 50 mixture of its two enantiomers
II. Stereoisomers that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other
III. The product has the same spatial arrangement of groups about the chiral carbon as the reactant
IV. The product has the opposite spatial arrangement about the chiral carbon, as in an SN2 reaction

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT defines retention (configuration kept), inversion (configuration reversed, typical of SN2), racemisation (equal amounts of both enantiomers, zero rotation, typical of SN1 at a chiral carbon) and enantiomers (non-superimposable mirror images).
solution.why_others_wrong: A-IV, B-III swaps retention and inversion. C-II, D-I swaps racemisation and enantiomers. A-I, C-III swaps retention and racemisation.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Haloalkanes and Haloarenes', stereochemical aspects of nucleophilic substitution
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the reactions of haloarenes are correct?

(a) Chlorobenzene is converted into phenol by heating with aqueous NaOH at 623 K and 300 atm.
(b) Chlorination of chlorobenzene (Cl₂, anhydrous FeCl₃) gives mainly o- and p-dichlorobenzene.
(c) Nitration of chlorobenzene gives mainly m-chloronitrobenzene.
(d) Haloarenes undergo SN1 reactions readily because the phenyl cation is stabilised by resonance.
(e) 2,4,6-Trinitrochlorobenzene is hydrolysed by warm water to 2,4,6-trinitrophenol.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Haloarenes need drastic conditions for nucleophilic substitution, but nitro groups at ortho/para positions make it easy (warm water suffices for the trinitro compound). Chlorine is ortho/para-directing in electrophilic substitution. The phenyl cation is not resonance-stabilised, so the SN1 route is ruled out.
steps: (e) three –NO₂ groups activate → picric acid → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Every other option includes (c) or (d), both false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Haloalkanes and Haloarenes', reactions of haloarenes

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Alkyl fluorides are best prepared by heating an alkyl chloride or bromide with a metallic fluoride such as AgF, Hg₂F₂, CoF₂ or SbF₃.
Reason (R): The C–F bond is the weakest of all the carbon–halogen bonds.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT states that alkyl fluorides are best made by the Swarts reaction. R is false: the C–F bond is the shortest and strongest carbon–halogen bond.
steps: R: C–F is the strongest C–X bond → false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Haloalkanes and Haloarenes', halogen exchange; nature of C–X bond
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 4.6 g of ethanol is converted into bromoethane with PBr₃. The bromoethane is converted into its Grignard reagent, which is treated with methanal, and the product is hydrolysed with dilute acid. Assuming every step is complete, the mass of the final alcohol is (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16):

solution.concept: Grignard reagent with methanal: a primary alcohol with one more carbon
solution.explanation: C₂H₅OH → C₂H₅Br → C₂H₅MgBr; with HCHO and hydrolysis, C₂H₅MgBr gives C₂H₅CH₂OH (propan-1-ol). One mole of ethanol gives one mole of propan-1-ol.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.6 g assumes the alcohol is ethanol again, ignoring the carbon added by methanal. 7.4 g is for a butanol (as if ethanal were used). 3.0 g halves the amount.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Haloalkanes and Haloarenes', Grignard reagents; Class 12 Chemistry, 'Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers', preparation of alcohols from Grignard reagents

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about nucleophilic substitution in alkyl halides are correct?

(a) (−)-2-Bromooctane reacts with OH⁻ by the SN2 mechanism to give (+)-octan-2-ol.
(b) SN1 reactions are generally carried out in polar protic solvents such as water, alcohol or ethanoic acid.
(c) 1-Bromobutane reacts faster than 2-bromobutane by the SN2 mechanism.
(d) Allyl chloride is less reactive than 1-chloropropane towards SN1 reactions.
(e) In SN1 reactions, the more stable the carbocation, the slower the reaction.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Factors in SN1 and SN2 reactions
solution.explanation: SN2 proceeds with inversion, as in NCERT's example of 2-bromooctane; it is fastest for the least hindered halide, so the primary bromide beats the secondary. SN1 needs a polar protic solvent to stabilise the ions, and its rate rises with carbocation stability, so the allyl halide (resonance-stabilised cation) is more reactive than 1-chloropropane.
steps: (d) allyl cation stabilised → more reactive → false
(e) more stable carbocation → faster SN1 → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Every other option includes (d) or (e), or leaves out (c) or (a).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Haloalkanes and Haloarenes', mechanism of nucleophilic substitution

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 1-Bromopropane is heated with alcoholic KOH to give X. X is treated with HBr in the absence of peroxide to give Y. Y is:

solution.explanation: Alcoholic KOH eliminates HBr to give propene. HBr then adds by Markovnikov's rule through the more stable secondary carbocation, putting Br on C-2.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1-Bromopropane would need peroxide (anti-Markovnikov addition). 1,2-Dibromopropane forms with Br₂, not HBr. Propan-2-ol would need acid-catalysed addition of water to X, not addition of HBr.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Haloalkanes and Haloarenes', elimination reactions; Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', Markovnikov's rule

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Propanone is reduced with sodium borohydride (NaBH₄). The product is:

solution.concept: Reduction of ketones to secondary alcohols
solution.explanation: Hydride reduction (NaBH₄, LiAlH₄) or catalytic hydrogenation turns the C=O of a ketone into CH–OH, giving a secondary alcohol.
solution.why_others_wrong: Propan-1-ol would come from propanal, not propanone. Propanal is not a reduction product of a ketone. Propane needs the Clemmensen or Wolff–Kishner reduction, not NaBH₄.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers', preparation of alcohols (reduction of aldehydes and ketones)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Methanol is also known as 'wood spirit' because it was earlier produced by:

solution.explanation: NCERT: methanol, also known as wood spirit, was produced by the destructive distillation of wood; today it is made by catalytic hydrogenation of carbon monoxide.
solution.why_others_wrong: Fermentation of sugars gives ethanol. Hydration of ethene also gives ethanol. Hydrolysis of methyl chloride is not how methanol was obtained historically.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers', some commercially important alcohols
solution.final_answer: Option C: destructive distillation of wood

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 18 g of glucose is fermented completely by the enzymes of yeast: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. The mass of ethanol formed is (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16):

solution.explanation: Each mole of glucose gives two moles of ethanol.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.6 g takes a 1 : 1 ratio. 18.0 g assumes the mass of glucose is all ethanol. 8.8 g is the mass of CO₂ formed.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers', ethanol (fermentation)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Ethoxyethane has a higher boiling point than butan-1-ol.
Statement II: Ethoxyethane and butan-1-ol have different molecular formulas.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Ethoxyethane (C₂H₅OC₂H₅) and butan-1-ol (C₄H₉OH) are both C₄H₁₀O, i.e. functional isomers. Ether molecules cannot hydrogen-bond with each other, so ethoxyethane boils far lower (about 308 K) than butan-1-ol (about 391 K).
steps: Statement I: no intermolecular H-bonding in ethers → lower b.p. → false
Statement II: both are C₄H₁₀O → false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers', physical properties of ethers
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The lower alcohols are readily soluble in water.
Reason (R): Alcohols can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: the solubility of alcohols in water is due to their ability to form hydrogen bonds with water. In the lower alcohols the small alkyl group does not prevent this, so they mix freely with water.
steps: –OH group forms H-bonds with H₂O → soluble (A true)
R gives this cause → R explains A
